A.explanation: About $40\text{ J}$ is far too small and is the order of kinetic energy of a slow-moving small object, not a $70\text{ kg}$ sprinter at $10\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

B.explanation: About $400\text{ J}$ is still a factor of 10 too small, corresponding for example to the same athlete moving at only about $3\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

C.explanation: Using $m \approx 70\text{ kg}$ and $v \approx 10\text{ m s}^{-1}$ gives $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 \approx 3500\text{ J}$, closest to $4000\text{ J}$.

D.explanation: About $40\,000\text{ J}$ is a factor of 10 too large and would need a speed over $30\text{ m s}^{-1}$ or a mass near $800\text{ kg}$.

hints: Start by estimating the two inputs for kinetic energy for a 100 m Olympic sprinter: a typical adult mass near $70\text{ kg}$ and a top speed from $100\text{ m}$ in about $10\text{ s}$.
Recall the governing relation $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$ in joules, so the $10\text{ m s}^{-1}$ speed is squared and then halved times the mass.
Calculate $0.5 \times 70 \times 10^2$ and compare the power of ten of your result with $40\text{ J}$, $400\text{ J}$, $4000\text{ J}$ and $40\,000\text{ J}$.
walkthrough: Identify what must be estimated: kinetic energy needs mass $m$ and speed $v$. An Olympic sprinter has $m \approx 70\text{ kg}$ to $80\text{ kg}$.
Estimate sprint speed from the 100 m race: $v \approx \text{distance} / \text{time} \approx 100\text{ m} / 10\text{ s} \approx 10\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
State the physical rule for translational kinetic energy: $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$ with $E_k$ in $\text{J}$, $m$ in $\text{kg}$ and $v$ in $\text{m s}^{-1}$.
Check order of magnitude: the result is a few thousand joules, so $40\text{ J}$ and $400\text{ J}$ are too small and $40\,000\text{ J}$ is too large by a factor of 10.
The closest reasonable estimate is $4000\text{ J}$. This is option C.
